meeting.who: The Bank of England (“the BoE”), the UK’s central bank. Its interest rate is set by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC): nine people, led by Governor Andrew Bailey. Five work at the Bank and four are “external” experts from outside. Each member votes, and the Bank publishes every vote by name, so we can see exactly who wanted what.

why_steps.title: The BoE has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: By law, the Bank of England’s main job is to keep prices steady. The government sets its target: prices should rise about 2% a year, measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI, from the Office for National Statistics, the ONS). If inflation moves more than 1 percentage point away from 2%, the Governor must write a public open letter to the Chancellor explaining why and what the Bank will do. Its main tool is Bank Rate, the interest rate the BoE pays banks on money they keep with it. It flows through to tracker mortgages, savings accounts and business loans. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Today Bank Rate is 4.00%, following the decision on November 5, 2026 (BoE).

why_steps.title: Prices are rising faster, led by energy and services
why_steps.html: Consumer prices were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 3.1% in August (ONS). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost £100 a year ago now costs about £103.50. The goal would be £102. The main driver remains energy costs. Motor fuel prices are up 29.8% in a year. Underneath, core prices (leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) rose to 2.8% from 2.6%, and prices of services such as haircuts, rents and restaurants ticked up to 3.7% from 3.4%. The BoE’s November Monetary Policy Report expects inflation to rise to around 5% by the middle of next year as higher energy prices continue to feed into bills (BoE).

why_steps.title: The real question: are energy costs spreading?
why_steps.html: The BoE cannot make oil cheaper. What it can do is stop a one-off jump in fuel turning into a lasting habit of rising prices. Economists call that spreading “second-round effects”: workers ask for bigger pay rises to cover their bills, firms raise prices to cover their wage and energy costs, and people start to expect high inflation as normal. Evidence from recent releases shows core CPI at 2.8% and services inflation at 3.7%. Firms in the BoE’s survey expect wage growth of 3.4% (DMP). The MPC noted that while direct energy effects are clear, there remains limited evidence of knock-on effects on other prices and wages so far.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoE might hold in December
why_steps.html:
• Rates just went up. The MPC increased Bank Rate to 4.00% in November, providing tighter policy stance to bear down on inflation.
  • Pay growth remains moderate overall. Regular pay growth stands at 3.7% with forward-looking expectations contained at 3.4%.
  • Job vacancies are cooling. Vacancies fell to 691,000 in September, showing some softening in employer demand (ONS).
  • Markets already pressed the brake. The 10-year gilt yield is 5.14%, keeping borrowing conditions restrictive.
  • The committee signaled a data-dependent pause. Policy is not on a pre-set path, and members will assess incoming evidence meeting by meeting.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoE might raise again
why_steps.html:
• Inflation is projected to hit 5% by the middle of next year according to the November Monetary Policy Report.
  • Pipeline pressures persist. Global energy prices remain elevated and motor fuel inflation sits at 29.8%.
  • Upside risks remain active. If second-round wage-price dynamics take root, further tightening may be required.
  • One member wanted more in November. One MPC member voted for a 0.5 percentage point increase to 4.25% in November.

why_steps.html: Following the November rate rise to 4.00%, the central bank is positioned to pause and evaluate incoming economic data. While inflation is projected to climb toward 5% next year due to energy shocks, the immediate policy tightening provides breathing room. That is why our probabilities stand at 70% Hold, 25% Raise and 5% Cut.

timeline.title: Holding at 4%, with the committee split
timeline.what: The MPC kept Bank Rate at 4% both times. In September the vote was 7–2. In November it was 5–4. In September the BoE also agreed to shrink its holdings of government bonds by £70 billion over the following year.
timeline.why: Inflation was high (3.8% in August 2025) but the BoE judged it had peaked.
timeline.people: Mortgage and savings rates stayed roughly the same.
timeline.because: one more soft inflation reading was enough to tip the balance.

timeline.title: A cut to 3.75%, by a single vote
timeline.what: The MPC lowered Bank Rate from 4% to 3.75%, by 5 votes to 4. Governor Bailey joined the four who had wanted a cut. The BoE said rates were likely to follow a gradual downward path.
timeline.why: Inflation had fallen to 3.2% in November, and the economy and job market looked soft.
timeline.people: Tracker and variable-rate mortgages got a little cheaper.

timeline.title: A pause, but still talking about cuts
timeline.what: Bank Rate stayed at 3.75%, by 5 votes to 4. The BoE said Bank Rate was likely to be reduced further.
timeline.why: Inflation was 3.4% in December, but the BoE expected it to fall toward 2% from April.
timeline.people: Borrowers were told cheaper loans were coming.
timeline.because: the BoE was preparing to cut when energy prices started soaring.

timeline.title: An energy shock: all nine vote to hold
timeline.what: All nine members voted to hold at 3.75%. The BoE noted that conflict in the Middle East caused a significant increase in global energy and commodity prices.
timeline.why: With energy prices jumping, cutting rates would have added fuel to inflation.
timeline.people: Petrol, diesel and household bills went up.
timeline.because: the debate flipped from when to cut to whether to raise.

timeline.title: The first votes for a rise
timeline.what: In April the vote was 8–1 to hold, with Huw Pill voting to raise. In June it was 7–2 as Megan Greene joined him.
timeline.why: Uncertainty over global energy prices prompted fears that waiting would let higher inflation take root.
timeline.people: Inflation eased temporarily, giving families relief.
timeline.because: each meeting added another member to the raise side.

timeline.title: Three votes to raise; oil had eased
timeline.what: The MPC held by 6 votes to 3; Catherine Mann joined Greene and Pill in wanting 4%. Inflation had dipped to 2.6% in June.
timeline.why: With oil temporarily lower, most members saw no immediate need to act.
timeline.people: The household energy price cap rose to £1,663 for July–September.

timeline.title: Held at 3.75% by 6–3, with an open letter
timeline.what: Same vote as July: Greene, Mann and Pill wanted 4%. Staff expected inflation of about 3¾% by year-end and slightly above 4% in early 2027. The Governor wrote an open letter to the Chancellor.
timeline.people: The energy price cap for October–December is set at £1,723.
timeline.because: inflation exceeded target by over 1 point, triggering an open letter.

timeline.title: Bank Rate increased to 4%
timeline.what: The MPC voted by a majority of 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00%. One member voted to increase Bank Rate by 0.5 percentage points to 4.25%.
timeline.why: Higher global energy prices and September CPI at 3.5% warranted tighter monetary policy.
timeline.people: Borrowers with tracker mortgages will see monthly repayments increase slightly.
timeline.because: our reading is that the BoE has stepped up to 4% and will now hold steady while monitoring inflation.

choices.title: Hold: keep Bank Rate at 4.00%
choices.meaning: the BoE maintains its newly increased rate while assessing how higher energy costs and past hikes ripple through the economy.
for: Rates just went up. Bank Rate was increased to 4.00% in November.
Pay and jobs remain mixed. Regular pay growth is 3.7% with cooling vacancies and unemployment at 4.7%.
Markets already tightened. The 10-year gilt rate is 5.14%, keeping borrowing conditions restrictive.
Data-dependent pause. The MPC indicated it will assess evidence meeting by meeting.
against: Oil prices remain very high ($107.03 a barrel for Brent).
Pipeline pressures could require further tightening if second-round effects spread.
choices.everyday: tracker mortgages and savings rates would stay at their current levels as the BoE pauses.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 4.25%
choices.meaning: the BoE acts further to combat rising inflation projections.
for: Inflation trajectory. MPR projects inflation reaching around 5% next year.
Persistent energy shock. High energy prices continue to push up headline figures.
Some members continue to favor a more aggressive tightening stance.
against: Bank Rate was just raised in November to 4.00%.
Limited evidence of knock-on wage pressures so far.
Economy is showing signs of cooling in retail sales and vacancies.
choices.everyday: borrowing costs would increase further, adding to household and business expenses.

choices.title: Cut: lower Bank Rate
choices.meaning: the BoE reverses course to support growth in the face of unexpected economic distress.
for: Only if a severe economic shock or financial crash occurred.
against: Inflation is rising toward 5%. Cutting would add fuel.
The BoE just raised rates in November.
The active debate is entirely about holding or raising further.
choices.everyday: loans would get cheaper, but such a move would contradict current inflation forecasts.

change.lead: Our 70% / 25% / 5% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The BoE can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before December 17 can change the December decision. A report released after it can only shape what happens next year.

gdp_first_estimate.why: Shows economic growth for July–September, helping gauge overall economic momentum.
gdp_first_estimate.trigger: Stronger growth leans toward holding at 4%; weaker growth could raise questions about policy tightness.

uk_labour_market_2.why: Will show whether the job market and wage growth are holding steady or softening.
uk_labour_market_2.trigger: Higher wage growth could revive hike expectations.

cpi.trigger: Higher-than-expected inflation keeps pressure on the BoE.

retail_sales_2.trigger: Soft retail sales indicate restrictive policy is working.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil, gas and the Middle East. Brent crude at $107.03 a barrel continues to drive inflation pressures.

report_card.one: CPI inflation rose to 3.5% in September, with services inflation at 3.7% and the BoE projecting inflation around 5% by mid-2027.
report_card.look: Consumer prices (CPI, up 3.5%), CPIH (up 3.6%), core CPI (2.8%), services (3.7%), and factory input prices.
report_card.why: Inflation is well above target following energy shocks, leading the BoE to raise Bank Rate to 4.00%.
report_card.change: Oil and gas prices falling back decisively alongside a drop in services inflation.
report_card.matters: Inflation projections reaching 5% are the core reason rates were raised.

report_card.one: Unemployment is at 4.7% and regular pay growth ticked up to 3.7%, while vacancies cooled to 691,000.
report_card.look: The unemployment rate, payroll jobs, job vacancies, and regular pay growth.
report_card.why: Unemployment ticked down to 4.7% for August and pay growth edged up to 3.7%, showing ongoing resilience alongside cooling vacancies.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising above 5% with falling pay growth → red.
report_card.matters: A balanced job market helps policymakers gauge second-round wage pressures.

report_card.one: The economy is growing modestly, but households remain cautious with a saving ratio of 8.8%.
report_card.look: GDP growth, monthly GDP, retail sales, and household saving.
report_card.why: Monthly GDP grew +0.1% in August and retail sales remain solid, but consumer caution persists.
report_card.change: Weak GDP figures and falling retail sales → red.
report_card.matters: Moderate growth gives the BoE room to assess its latest rate hike.

report_card.one: Government borrowing costs remain elevated with 10-year gilt yields at 5.14%.
report_card.look: Gilt yields, SONIA, sterling exchange rates, and lending conditions.
report_card.why: 10-year gilt yields at 5.14% and 5-year yields at 4.78% keep borrowing conditions tight.
report_card.change: Gilt yields settling back toward 5% → yellow.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates slow the economy, doing some of the BoE's tightening work.

said.v: Increased Bank Rate to 4.00%, 8 votes to 1
w: What it said: The MPC voted 8–1 to increase Bank Rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4%. One member voted for 4.25%. Inflation is expected to rise to around 5% by mid-next year.
Why it matters: reflects determined action against energy-driven inflation pressures.
What it said: Bailey, Breeden, Dhingra, Lombardelli, Ramsden and Taylor voted to hold. Greene, Mann and Pill voted to raise to 4%. The Committee noted risks to inflation are tilted to the upside.
Why it matters: preceded the November hike to 4%.

said.v: Assessing labor market slack and wage pressures
w: What it said: Greene examined whether labor market slack is sufficient to mitigate the latest supply shock and restrain wage-setting second-round effects.
Why it matters: highlights ongoing hawkish scrutiny against lingering inflation.

said.v: Leaning toward tightening if energy prices persist
w: What she said: policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.
Why it matters: signaled support for the subsequent November tightening.
What he said: interest rates may need to rise even as economic activity weakens.
Why it matters: foreshadowed the Governor joining the majority to raise rates in November.

said.pv: Voted to raise in July and September
w: What she said: our current monetary policy stance is not sufficiently tight, and she cannot take comfort from tighter financial market conditions.
Why it matters: consistent hawk on the committee.

group_intros.prices: These numbers show how fast prices are rising. The BoE’s target is 2% a year for CPI. With September CPI at 3.5% and the BoE projecting inflation around 5% next year, the BoE watches closely for second-round effects.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the BoE has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date UK consumer price series (its OECD copy stops in March 2025), so for prices use the ONS directly. FRED’s UK 10-year gilt rate is a monthly average and its unemployment and GDP copies arrive months late, so they may differ from the daily and latest figures on this page.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website, or on the Bank of England’s own statistics database.
